title: A Holistic View of Volatility | Dimensional
gist: Dimensional argues that standalone volatility statistics mislead: global small caps ran a 17.93% annualized standard deviation from January 1999 to June 2026 versus 15.30% for global large caps, yet blending small into large produced portfolio standard deviations very close to large caps alone while returns rose meaningfully with small cap weight. The piece extends the same 'don't judge risk in a vacuum' logic to private markets, where return smoothing mechanically understates reported volatility.

insights.claim: Dimensional argues that the variability an investor actually experiences is a property of the whole portfolio, not of its individual asset categories, so judging any sleeve by its standalone volatility is the wrong test.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Screen allocations on marginal contribution to total portfolio risk rather than on the sleeve's own standard deviation, or you will systematically under-own volatile-but-diversifying assets.
insights.quote: But the variability of an investor’s account balance depends on the entirety of the portfolio, not its individual components.

insights.claim: Because small cap stocks behave differently from large cap stocks, adding small caps to a large cap portfolio delivered a diversification benefit that left the combined portfolio's standard deviation very similar to that of large caps alone.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: The apparent risk cost of a small cap allocation largely disappears at the portfolio level, so an investor avoiding small caps for volatility reasons is paying for risk reduction they never received.
insights.quote: The net effect for combining large and small caps is standard deviations very similar to the large caps themselves.

insights.claim: Dimensional frames risk and return statistics viewed in isolation as an incomplete recipe for evaluating any asset category, a general standard it applies across both public and private assets.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Treat single-asset Sharpe ratios and standard deviations in manager pitches as insufficient evidence; demand the correlation and portfolio-blend analysis before sizing.
insights.quote: for any asset category, risk and return statistics in isolation do not provide a complete recipe to evaluate it

insights.claim: From January 1999 to June 2026, a global small cap index posted an annualized standard deviation of 17.93% versus 15.30% for global large caps, a gap of roughly 2.6 percentage points.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: The standalone volatility premium for small caps over a 27-year global sample is real but modest, a useful anchor when a risk model assumes a much larger penalty.
insights.quote: the annualized standard deviation of a global small cap index from January 1999 to June 2026 was 17.93%, compared to 15.30% for global large caps

insights.claim: Over the January 1999 to June 2026 global equity sample, returns increased meaningfully as portfolio weight in small caps increased, while combined portfolio volatility did not rise commensurately.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: The historical trade-off favored tilting toward small caps: incremental return without proportional incremental portfolio risk, which is the empirical case for a size tilt.
insights.quote: Returns, on the other hand, meaningfully increased with increasing weight in small caps.

themes.theme: Private market volatility is an artifact of measurement

insights.claim: Dimensional holds that return smoothing in private markets renders their reported volatility metrics less meaningful, and treats the public-market small cap example as the same measurement problem in a different setting.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Discount low reported private-market volatility when setting allocations; the diversification and risk-budget benefits credited to private assets may be measurement artifacts rather than economics.
insights.quote: Last week, we highlighted how return smoothing in private markets makes their volatility metrics less meaningful.
insights.locator: Last week, we highlighted how return

insights.claim: The mechanism behind smoothed private-market volatility is periodic rather than continuous valuation, which dampens observed short-term price fluctuations and mechanically lowers reported return variability.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Adjust private-asset volatility upward (or use desmoothed series) before running mean-variance optimization, otherwise the optimizer will over-allocate to private assets by construction.
insights.quote: Private market assets are valued only periodically, which can appear to dampen short-term price fluctuations and make returns appear to have lower volatility.

insights.claim: Dimensional points out that Harry Markowitz established the case for evaluating volatility at the portfolio level rather than asset by asset roughly 70 years ago in Modern Portfolio Theory, implying investors still routinely violate a seven-decade-old principle.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: The persistence of siloed risk evaluation is itself the opportunity: assets penalized for standalone volatility can be structurally cheap to diversified holders.
insights.quote: The Nobel laureate Harry Markowitz spelled this out 70 years ago in his Modern Portfolio Theory framework.
